scenes.title: hook (five and a half hours, or forty minutes)

voiceover.text: So, what should athletes eat and drink, and when? Two athletes finish at the same venue on the same day. One has swum nineteen kilometres in five and a half hours. The other has played a forty-minute netball match. Both are told to eat and drink properly. Write down the three biggest differences in what they actually need, and why. Then decide: is the difference mainly about what they eat, or when?

scenes.title: carbohydrate is the fuel that runs out

voiceover.text: In Year 11 you saw that glycogen, the carbohydrate stored in muscle and liver, is a small, fast store, and fat is a huge, slow one. When glycogen runs low, intensity has to drop, and that's hitting the wall. You also saw that training, not extra protein, is what builds muscle. So nearly every nutrition decision is about timing carbohydrate.

The dot point names three windows, and each has a different job. Before performance, the aim is to start with full glycogen, good hydration and a settled stomach. That means a carbohydrate-rich meal, moderate in protein and low in fat and fibre, about three to four hours before, plus a small snack nearer if needed. A big fatty meal too close to the start sits in the stomach, because fat and fibre slow its emptying. During performance, the aim is to delay running out. For events longer than about an hour, take carbohydrate that's easy to swallow, plus fluid. For short events, you usually need nothing, because the glycogen you start with lasts that long. After performance, replace glycogen, add protein for repair, and replace fluid and sodium. How urgent that is depends on the next effort. Carbohydrate loading, raising glycogen above normal over the days before, only suits long, continuous events, because a fuller store only helps if the event would otherwise reach the wall. And try nothing new on competition day.

scenes.title: fluid: two errors in opposite directions

voiceover.text: Sweating is how the body sheds heat, so losing fluid is the price of staying cool. In Year 11 you saw sweat shrink the plasma, so stroke volume falls and heart rate drifts up. What matters here is what that does to performance. Core temperature climbs faster, effort feels harder, and decisions and skill get worse too. That's dehydration. But the opposite error is more dangerous. Drink far more than you lose, and blood sodium is diluted. That's hyponatraemia, most often seen in slower participants in long events who drink at every station. In severe cases it can be life-threatening. So the goal isn't to drink as much as possible. It's to replace roughly what you lose.

So how much is that? Sweat rates vary a lot between people, so measure them. Weigh the athlete before a session, dry. Record everything they drink. Weigh them again straight after, towelled dry. Sweat loss is the weight lost plus the fluid drunk. Say an athlete goes from seventy kilograms to sixty-eight point eight in an hour and a half, drinking point eight of a litre. That's one point two plus point eight, two litres of sweat, or about one point three litres an hour. They're still one point two kilograms down, and some of what they drink is lost as urine, so aim to drink about one and a half times that, around one point eight litres, with some sodium. And repeat it in different conditions, because heat raises sweat rate. The physiology is general, but the numbers are individual.

Different sports don't need a memorised menu. They need three questions: how long, how hard, and when can the athlete refuel? The open-water swimmer goes five hours or more, moderately hard, and can only feed at boat stops. So carbohydrate loading makes sense, carbohydrate and fluid at every feed, rehearsed in training, and sodium matters. The netballer plays under an hour, hard and stop-start, with only breaks. So a normal well-fuelled diet, a light carbohydrate meal beforehand, fluid at the breaks, and little else for one match. And in a multi-day tournament, the recovery meal is also tomorrow's pre-game meal, so the windows merge. That answers the hook: it's mostly about when. And "using research" means judging claims. Ask who made it and whether they profit, who was studied, what was actually measured, and how big the effect was.
Two things to remember. Carbohydrate is the fuel that runs out. And for any sport, ask duration, intensity, opportunity.

scenes.title: attempt one (a rower and a cyclist)

voiceover.text: Two exam questions. First. A seventeen-year-old rows a two-thousand-metre heat in the morning, and the final in the afternoon. A cyclist rides a four-and-a-half-hour road race on a thirty-four-degree day. For each, analyse the three variables, then outline what they need before, during and after. Pause here to answer.

The rower's race lasts about seven minutes, very hard, so fuel isn't the limit during it. But the gap before the final makes recovery urgent: carbohydrate and fluid soon after the heat. The cyclist faces hours in heat, so carbohydrate loading, carbohydrate and fluid with sodium throughout, matched to their sweat rate. The classic mistake is giving both the same plan.

Second. A runner weighs sixty-two kilograms before a seventy-five-minute session and sixty point nine after, having drunk point six of a litre. Calculate their sweat rate per hour, and state how much fluid they should aim to drink afterwards, and why. Pause here to answer.

Mass lost is one point one kilograms, plus point six of a litre drunk, so one point seven litres of sweat. Divide by one and a quarter hours: about one point four litres an hour. They're still one point one down, so drink about one and a half times that, around one point seven litres, with some sodium, because some is lost as urine. The classic mistake is forgetting to add the fluid they drank.

So time carbohydrate to when it's needed, replace roughly the fluid you lose, and plan from duration, intensity and opportunity. But the after window doesn't stop when the meal is eaten. It runs on into the night, where most recovery actually happens. How do sleep, food and fluid work together to cut fatigue and injury?
